item.title: One Shot, Six Months, Ten Countries: Why the World's Best HIV Prevention Drug Isn't Reaching Everyone Who Needs It
item.body:
## A Breakthrough Drug Meets a Familiar Bottleneck

For decades, HIV prevention has meant daily pills, regular clinic visits, and the kind of routine that's easy to fall off of. Lenacapavir, the twice-yearly injectable developed by Gilead Sciences, was supposed to change that math entirely. Two shots a year, near-complete protection in clinical trials, and a level of convenience that public health researchers have called one of the most significant advances in HIV prevention in a generation.

The catch isn't the science. It's getting the drug into arms.

## What Gilead Promised

Under pressure from global health advocates and in partnership with international health organizations, Gilead agreed to supply lenacapavir at no profit to a group of low- and middle-income countries where HIV rates remain highest, particularly across parts of sub-Saharan Africa. The company also licensed generic manufacturers to produce lower-cost versions for broader distribution once regulatory approvals and production capacity catch up.

On paper, it was a rare example of a pharmaceutical company moving quickly to align pricing with public health need rather than waiting years for generic competition to force the issue.

## Where the Rollout Is Stalling

In practice, according to clinicians and health officials involved in early distribution, the picture has been uneven. Some clinics in participating countries report shelves stocked with the injectable and ready to enroll patients. Others say they've been told to expect shipments only as late as November, leaving providers unable to give patients a firm timeline and, in some cases, unable to start new patients on the drug at all.

Health workers describe a mix of causes: limited global manufacturing capacity for a genuinely new type of injectable, regulatory approval processes that move at different speeds from country to country, and the logistical complexity of distributing a temperature-sensitive product across health systems with very different levels of infrastructure. None of these are unusual problems in global drug rollouts — but they are colliding with unusually high expectations for a drug that trial data suggested could meaningfully bend the trajectory of new HIV infections.

## Why the Timing Matters

Public health advocates note that delays are not neutral. Every month a clinic goes without supply is a month where people who might have started prevention instead go without it, relying on daily pills that are effective but harder to sustain for many people over long periods. International health organizations have been vocal about wanting the initial rollout to reach the countries and populations most affected by HIV as quickly as possible, arguing that early, well-targeted access can have outsized effects on transmission over time.

Gilead and its distribution partners have generally acknowledged that scaling manufacturing and logistics for a first-of-its-kind product takes time, and have pointed to expansion plans intended to close gaps between countries in the coming months.

## The Bigger Picture

Lenacapavir's rollout is being closely watched not just as a public health story but as a test case for how quickly the industry can move when a company commits to no-profit pricing in lower-income markets. If the supply chain smooths out in the coming months, advocates say it could become a model for future drug launches. If the gaps persist into next year, it risks becoming another example of a promising medical breakthrough arriving unevenly — available in theory long before it's available in practice.

For now, the answer likely varies clinic by clinic. Some patients in eligible countries can get an appointment for lenacapavir this month. Others are being asked to check back after the new year begins its final stretch, hoping the supply catches up with the science.
